subject: Environment
topic: Water pollution and management — mixed tiers
description: BOD, COD, eutrophication, Namami Gange, conventions

questions.stem: 'Eutrophication' of a water body refers to:

options.option_text: Depletion of oxygen due to thermal pollution
Excessive nutrient enrichment causing algal blooms
Salinisation from agricultural runoff
Plastic accumulation in rivers

questions.explanation: Eutrophication — large amounts of nitrates and phosphates (from sewage, detergents, fertiliser runoff) fuel rapid algal and plant growth. When the algae die, their decomposition by bacteria uses up dissolved oxygen, causing fish kills and 'dead zones'. Classic example — toxic cyanobacterial blooms in Lake Erie. The Baltic Sea and parts of the Gulf of Mexico also have seasonal dead zones.

questions.stem: BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) is a measure of the amount of dissolved oxygen required by:

options.option_text: Fish and aquatic plants for respiration
Aerobic micro-organisms to decompose organic matter
Aerobic algae during photosynthesis
Chemical oxidation of minerals

questions.explanation: BOD — oxygen consumed by aerobic bacteria over 5 days at 20 °C while they break down organic pollutants (sewage, food waste). Clean rivers have BOD < 3 mg/L; heavily polluted ones may exceed 30 mg/L. COD (Chemical Oxygen Demand) oxidises everything oxidisable (organic + some inorganic) with strong chemicals and is always higher than BOD. High BOD → fish die.

questions.stem: The 'Namami Gange' programme, launched by the Government of India, is focused on:

options.option_text: Bore-well recharge in Tamil Nadu
Cleaning and conservation of the Ganga river
Afforestation in the Himalayas
Wetland protection in the Sundarbans

questions.explanation: Namami Gange — ~₹20,000-crore programme launched in 2014 — aims at cleaning and conservation of the Ganga through sewage-treatment plants, industrial-effluent control, river-front development, afforestation, public awareness and biodiversity conservation. The National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG) is the implementing body. Precursor schemes were the Ganga Action Plan (GAP-I 1985, GAP-II 1993).

questions.stem: Minamata disease — serious neurological damage caused by long-term water pollution — is caused by which heavy metal?

options.option_text: Lead
Mercury
Cadmium
Arsenic

questions.explanation: Minamata disease — documented in Minamata, Japan in the 1950s — was caused by methylmercury discharged into Minamata Bay by a chemical plant and biomagnified through the fish consumed by the local population. Symptoms — ataxia, loss of peripheral vision, muscle weakness, damage to the foetus. The Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013) is the global instrument that bans / phases-out mercury uses. Itai-itai disease (also Japan) — caused by cadmium pollution.

questions.stem: Widespread groundwater contamination by arsenic in India is especially severe in:

options.option_text: Rajasthan and Gujarat
West Bengal and Bihar
Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh
Punjab and Haryana

questions.explanation: Arsenic contamination of shallow groundwater is a major health issue in the Bengal-Bihar Ganga basin, and also affects Jharkhand, UP, Assam, Manipur. It is released naturally from alluvial aquifer sediments. Long-term exposure causes skin lesions, peripheral neuropathy and cancer. Fluoride contamination is more severe in Rajasthan, Gujarat, AP and parts of TN. Punjab faces arsenic in patches and uranium in deeper aquifers.

questions.stem: The Ramsar Convention (1971) is an international treaty for the conservation of:

options.option_text: Endangered primates
Wetlands of international importance
Marine mammals
Transboundary rivers

questions.explanation: The Ramsar Convention (signed in Ramsar, Iran, 1971; in force 1975) protects wetlands of international importance. Sites listed under it are called 'Ramsar sites'. India has over 80 Ramsar sites, including Chilika Lake (Odisha), Keoladeo (Rajasthan), Loktak (Manipur) and the Sundarbans (West Bengal). Wetland services — flood regulation, aquifer recharge, fish nurseries, biodiversity.

questions.stem: Drinking-water with fluoride far above the safe limit of 1.5 mg/L causes which disease?

options.option_text: Scurvy
Fluorosis
Goitre
Beri-beri

questions.explanation: Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis (mottling of teeth) and, in severe chronic cases, skeletal fluorosis (bone deformities, joint pain). Severely affected states — Rajasthan, AP, TN, Gujarat, UP, MP. Scurvy is caused by vitamin-C deficiency; goitre by iodine deficiency; beri-beri by vitamin-B₁ (thiamine) deficiency. Small amounts of fluoride prevent tooth decay (hence its use in toothpaste). dental and skeletal.

questions.stem: Which microorganism is internationally accepted as the standard indicator of fecal contamination in drinking water quality testing?

options.option_text: Escherichia coli, a gram-negative rod-shaped intestinal bacterium
Vibrio cholerae, the primary causative agent of cholera disease
Staphylococcus aureus, commonly found on human skin surfaces
Salmonella typhi, the bacterium responsible for causing typhoid fever

questions.explanation: E. coli is present in vast numbers in human intestines and reliably signals recent fecal contamination when found in water — making it the globally accepted indicator organism. Vibrio cholerae, Salmonella typhi, and Staphylococcus aureus are pathogens but are not used as standard fecal indicators because their absence does not guarantee water safety.

questions.stem: The discharge of hot water effluents from thermal power plants into rivers primarily harms aquatic ecosystems by:

options.option_text: Increasing dissolved oxygen, making the water toxic for sensitive fish species
Decreasing dissolved oxygen, causing thermal stress and suffocation in aquatic life
Raising the pH drastically, turning river water strongly alkaline for organisms
Depositing heavy metal sediment accumulation along the entire river bed

questions.explanation: Warm water has lower dissolved oxygen solubility than cold water, so thermal discharges reduce DO levels, suffocating fish and other aquatic organisms — this is thermal pollution. Option A is a classic reversal error: higher temperature means lower dissolved oxygen, not higher. pH and heavy metals are unrelated to thermal discharges.

questions.stem: Chemical Oxygen Demand (COD) is considered a more comprehensive water quality parameter than BOD because COD measures:

options.option_text: Oxygen needed by aerobic bacteria to decompose only biodegradable organic matter
Oxygen demand covering both biodegradable and non-biodegradable organic substances
Amount of dissolved oxygen present in the water sample at a specific temperature
Oxygen consumed during photosynthesis by submerged aquatic plants in river systems

questions.explanation: COD uses a strong chemical oxidant (potassium dichromate) to oxidize all organic matter — including non-biodegradable industrial chemicals that microbes cannot break down — making COD ≥ BOD for any sample. Option A describes BOD, not COD. Option C describes dissolved oxygen (DO), a completely different parameter.

questions.stem: Excess nitrates in groundwater cause 'Blue Baby Syndrome' (Methemoglobinemia) in infants. Which is the most common agricultural source of this nitrate contamination?

options.option_text: Excessive application of nitrogen-based chemical fertilizers on agricultural land
Discharge of untreated domestic sewage from urban households into open fields
Industrial effluents carrying heavy metals like lead and cadmium into soil
Seepage of petroleum hydrocarbons from underground fuel storage tank leakages

questions.explanation: Urea and ammonium nitrate fertilizers leach nitrates into groundwater. In infants, gut bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite, which binds haemoglobin forming methemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport and causing bluish skin. Heavy metals (C) and petroleum (D) cause entirely different toxicological effects. Sewage (B) also adds nitrates but the dominant agricultural vector is chemical fertilizers — the standard PYQ-tested answer.

questions.stem: In a conventional sewage treatment plant, biological decomposition of dissolved organic matter by aerobic microorganisms occurs during which treatment stage?

options.option_text: Primary treatment, which removes large suspended solids through physical sedimentation
Secondary treatment, where aerobic microbes biologically degrade dissolved organic waste
Tertiary treatment, involving advanced nutrient removal and chemical disinfection methods
Pre-treatment stage, which only screens out coarse grit and heavy floating debris

questions.explanation: Secondary treatment — via activated sludge process or trickling filters — uses aerobic bacteria to biodegrade dissolved organics, dramatically reducing BOD. Primary treatment is purely physical (screening + settling). Tertiary is polishing via chemical or membrane methods. Confusing secondary with primary is the most common exam mistake on this topic.

questions.stem: Itai-Itai disease, the first documented mass cadmium poisoning through water and soil contamination, was reported from which river basin?

options.option_text: Jinzu River basin in Toyama Prefecture, downstream of zinc mine operations
Sumida River basin near Tokyo, polluted by upstream chemical factory discharges
Agano River basin in Niigata, associated with mercury-based industrial effluents
Tamagawa River basin in Kanagawa, severely contaminated by lead smelter wastewater

questions.explanation: Itai-Itai ('it hurts-it hurts') disease struck residents of the Jinzu River valley in Toyama during the 1950s–60s, caused by cadmium discharged by Mitsui Mining's zinc smelter accumulating in rice and water. Option C is the classic distractor: the Agano River basin in Niigata is linked to Niigata Minamata disease — caused by mercury, not cadmium.

questions.stem: The 'oxygen sag curve' plotted for a river at successive points downstream of a sewage outfall correctly represents which ecological phenomenon?

options.option_text: A steady rise in dissolved oxygen as organic nutrients boost aquatic plant productivity
A sharp DO dip followed by gradual recovery as river self-purification slowly proceeds
A continuous irreversible decline in dissolved oxygen from the outfall to the sea
Cyclic daily fluctuation of dissolved oxygen driven entirely by seasonal temperature swings

questions.explanation: Sewage input triggers rapid bacterial decomposition that depletes dissolved oxygen (DO) to a critical minimum — the 'sag'. Further downstream, as organic load is exhausted and atmospheric re-aeration resumes, DO recovers toward saturation — demonstrating the river's natural self-purification capacity. Option A confuses the sag with eutrophication's daytime photosynthesis peak. Option C is wrong because recovery always occurs given sufficient river length and dilution.
